To this end, we only needed a total of 154 polaron barrier calculations, out of 3649 symmetry inequivalent ones, achieving an over 20-fold increase of computational efficiency. Overall, our work demonstrates how DFT-trained ML surrogates can be used to quantitatively and efficiently sample the dynamics of small polarons in energy materials.

title: ADfiRe: An empirical- and CFD-informed advection-diffusion-reaction thermal model for wildfire spread
abstract: Real-time wildfire forecasting requires a trade-off between rapid yet physically relevant models and high fidelity but computationally costly models of flame spread over heterogeneous, multiphase solid fuel. The present study introduces ADfiRe, a hybrid framework that integrates empirical correlations and CFD-informed parameterizations into a physics-based advection-diffusion-reaction (ADR) formulation. The key features of ADfiRe are the use of established fuel databases, the capacity to handle multiple fuels, and a methodology to capture the effect of arbitrary topography. Furthermore, it includes the effect of flame tilting due to wind, thus accounting for the differences between plume- and wind-dominated fire propagation. ADfiRe resolves explicitly the coupled thermochemical degradation as well as heat and mass transport mechanisms of the advancing fire front. The wind field is modeled based on an appropriately defined Byram number. The model is validated against five well-documented experimental field-scale fires in Mediterranean shrublands, showing quantitative agreement with key metrics such as the rate of spread (ROS) and the fireline intensity, through a two-stage, Arrhenius-based heterogeneous reaction scheme coupling solid-fuel pyrolysis and oxygen-limited char/volatile combustion.

title: Functional Cooperation between Pt Single Atoms and Nanoparticles on TiO 2 for Photocatalytic Dehydrogenation and C–C Coupling
abstract: Dehydrogenative coupling reactions that activate inert C–H bonds for C–C bond formation remain challenging because of unfavorable thermodynamics and kinetics without external oxidants. We report a hybrid photocatalytic system consisting of mixed Pt species on TiO2 (Ptmix/TiO2) combined with the hydrogen atom transfer reagent 2,2,2-trichloroethanol (TCE) for the dehydrogenative coupling of toluene. The system delivers 11% toluene conversion with 94% selectivity to bibenzyl and stoichiometric H2 evolution.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Pressure-driven evolution of crystal and molecular structures reshapes excited-state competition in coronene
abstract: Molecular nanocarbons exhibit unique optoelectronic properties and considered as promising candidates for organic device applications, however, understanding how molecular geometry and crystal packing jointly govern physical properties remains a fundamental challenge in π-conjugated molecular materials. Here, we demonstrate how these structural factors modulate the photoluminescence of coronene under high pressure. Combining high-pressure single-crystal X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, optical spectroscopy, and density functional theory calculations, we establish a relationship between distinct structural changes and the evolution of competing emissive states. Our results reveal that crystal polymorphism modifies the balance between free-exciton (FE) and self-trapped-exciton (STE) emission, while pressure-induced molecular bending is associated with a nonmonotonic evolution of STE emission. As intermolecular distances shorten, enhanced intermolecular electronic interactions give rise to excimer-related emission, introducing an additional emissive pathway. Although pressure-dependent optical properties of coronene have been linked to changes in crystal packing, our findings highlight that the optical response of a molecular solid is not governed by molecular deformation or crystal packing alone, but emerges from their interplay with intermolecular electronic coupling. By directly resolving molecular bending alongside changes in excited-state emission, this work provides insight into how distinct structural degrees of freedom can reshape the photophysical behavior of π-conjugated molecular solids.

title: Electric Fields Turn Vacancy-trapping Grain Boundaries into Li-Ion Pathways in Li2O
abstract: Ion transport in solids has conventionally been understood from equilibrium diffusion, yet ions in batteries are driven by electric fields. Does field-driven ion transport follow equilibrium behavior? We examined this question in bulk Li2O and at its grain boundaries (GBs) using electric-field molecular dynamics combining a machine learning interatomic potential with a Bader charge prediction model. Although Li diffusion in cubic Li2O is isotropic at zero field, an electric field renders it orientation dependent because Li hops along a limited set of crystallographic pathways that the field biases unequally. At GBs, this anisotropy becomes a qualitative difference: a GB that strongly traps Li vacancies but exhibits a strong field response releases them under a field, whereas a weakly responsive GB retains them despite weaker vacancy trapping. These results show that field-driven GB transport is governed not by static thermodynamics alone but by the angle between the electric field and the diffusion pathways of the constituent grains.

title: Crystal Structure Prediction from Search to Learning: A 30-Year Expedition
abstract: Crystal structure prediction (CSP) determines periodic atomic or molecular arrangements from chemical composition and physical conditions. Over three decades, CSP has evolved from chemical construction and global energy optimization to hybrid approaches combining symmetry, learned potentials, adaptive search, and deep generative models. This survey reviews method, software, review, and benchmark records from 1996 to October 2026, covering inorganic and molecular crystals, including formula-conditioned diffusion, flow, and autoregressive models that preserve composition. We classify methods by candidate construction and exploration: template and discrete construction, random search, evolutionary search, swarm and differential evolution, energy-landscape exploration, adaptive machine-learning-guided search, and learned generation. We distinguish representation, relaxation, ranking, and physical qualification. Benchmarks reveal no universally dominant approach. In a 46-target leaderboard snapshot, the best-performing template method achieves higher top-1 recovery than leading generative models, but paired tests show no statistically significant differences from several generative competitors. We also audit predictions for 68 experimentally examined materials, including 52 with structures confirmed by diffraction or microscopy. Predictions for 23 of the 68 preceded experiment, mostly through first-principles global search. Within the reviewed evidence, we find no independently confirmed discovery in which a deep generative model predicted the structure before experiment. We conclude with the principal limitations of current CSP algorithms and priorities for future research.

title: Classifier-Guided Latent Diffusion for Small-Molecule Generation
abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a promising class of generative models for molecular design because of their ability to learn complex chemical distributions and support conditional or guided generation. In this work, we investigate a latent diffusion pipeline for property-guided small-molecule generation. The proposed framework represents canonicalized SMILES strings using a frozen ChemBERTa encoder, trains a Transformer-based decoder to reconstruct SELFIES strings from molecular latent embeddings, and learns an unconditional denoising diffusion model in the ChemBERTa latent space. To enable property-directed generation, a differentiable latent property predictor is used to guide the diffusion sampling process. Generated SELFIES strings are converted to SMILES, validated using RDKit, and evaluated using molecular validity, uniqueness, novelty, and predicted property scores. We study guidance toward two drug-relevant binary endpoints: blood--brain barrier permeability and inhibition of human $β$-secretase 1. The results suggest that latent diffusion over pretrained molecular embeddings can generate chemically valid and novel molecules while enabling controllable steering toward desired molecular properties.

title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture
abstract: Phase-field simulation of thermally driven fracture requires resolving localized crack bands whose paths are unknown in advance and thermal boundary layers whose thickness evolves during the transient. Neural energy-based computations of thermal fracture have so far started from defects placed in advance. This paper proposes a mesh-free deep energy method based on multiresolution neural representations that predicts spontaneous crack nucleation, crack spacing, and selective crack propagation and arrest under transient thermal loading. Two networks, each with its own multiresolution encoding, represent the displacement and phase fields and the transient temperature, and the mechanical energy and the incremental functional of the backward Euler heat equation are estimated on integration points redrawn at every iteration. Restricting irreversibility to the crack set, carrying the optimizer state across load steps and decaying the learning rates within each step help prevent spurious damage accumulation. On two notched plates the initiation peak loads agree closely with an independent finite element reference. On a quenched glass strip under an analytical temperature field the crack path changes from straight to oscillatory and then to branched, with an oscillation threshold close to the linear stability prediction. Under a prescribed boundary temperature a quenched ceramic slab forms a crack array of the type observed in experiment, with a spacing close to that of a published benchmark. On the slab and a quenched annulus the arrays are denser than those of a finite element computation on the same material field. No crack paths, nucleation sites or crack-adapted meshes are prescribed.

title: Machine-learning charge density for electronic materials and devices simulation
abstract: We present a machine-learning (ML) charge density model, DeltaChargeNet, integrated with the full-potential tight-binding muffin-tin orbital (FP-TB-MTO) method for electronic structure and quantum transport simulations of materials and devices. The ML model predicts electron density from atomic structures with low linear-scaling cost, while FP-TB-MTO provides an accurate tight-binding representation of the system Hamiltonian. To achieve high-fidelity ML density for complex devices with interfaces and disorder, we train an equivariant graph convolutional network to predict $Δρ$-the difference between DFT and atomic superposition densities-under a charge neutrality constraint required for inhomogeneous systems. A secondary ML residual charge model compensates for errors in the primary $Δρ$ model. The predicted density is then used within the full-relativistic FP-TB-MTO framework combined with the non-equilibrium Green's function method. We validate our method on bulk HgCdTe disordered alloys (including vacancy defects) and Au/HgCdTe/Au disordered devices. The maximum band energy error is below 10 meV for bulk HgCdTe. For devices, the charge neutrality constraint suppresses long-wavelength charge bias that would otherwise distort the electrostatic potential by 0.68-1.88 eV near the device center, while residual compensation corrects the remaining 0.16-0.46 eV potential mismatch, essential for reproducing the correct potential barrier profile. Together, these corrections reproduce the layer-resolved potential, including interface steps and bulk-like plateaus, within 0.1 eV of fully self-consistent DFT. Finally, we demonstrate quantum transport in a 11220-atom infrared detector. By combining first-principles accuracy with linear-scaling inference, DeltaChargeNet enables large-scale device simulations without the full DFT self-consistent field loop.

title: Unified constitutive model of body-centered cubic metals informed by discrete dislocation dynamics
abstract: Predicting plastic flow in body-centered cubic metals across temperature and strain-rate regimes requires distinguishing structural resistance from kinetic contributions. Here, we develop a temperature dependent mobility law for screw dislocation, integrating thermal activation theory and relativistic effects. Through discrete dislocation dynamics simulations, uniaxial tension and compression simulations were conducted on configurations with different initial dislocation densities, elucidating the correlation between plastic strain rate and key parameters such as stress, temperature, and dislocation density. Subsequently, a unified constitutive model incorporating temperature and strain rate is derived based on microscopic mechanisms. The model naturally bridges microscopic mechanisms to continuum response, resolving the additivity dilemma by establishing explicit physical criteria for how structural resistances and competing kinetic mechanisms superimpose. Through rigorous bottom-up simulations, we quantitatively capture the crossover point where phonon drag overtakes thermal activation, providing a mechanism-based explanation of anomalous thermal hardening. This work enables physically consistent predictions of strength and creep behavior across broad temperature and strain-rate regimes, advancing beyond phenomenological descriptions toward transparent, mechanism-based alloy design.

title: Data-driven exploration of the strength-ductility synergy in refractory high-entropy alloys
abstract: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have attracted increasing attention for their exceptional ability to retain strength at high temperatures. However, current research mainly concentrates on compositions close to equimolar alloys, leaving a large part of the composition space unexplored. Here, we develop a multiscale framework based on a data-driven dislocation genome method that constructs energy landscapes for edge dislocation motion across various compositions. The local configurational force derived from the energy landscape is incorporated into dislocation dynamics simulations, revealing a scaling law connecting macroscale strength and atomic-scale local resistance governed by fluctuations in the local configurational force. Based on this scaling law, a new solid-solution strengthening model for edge dislocation in BCC alloys is developed, followed by a data-driven exploration of refractory alloys considering both strength and ductility. The developed method and theory are adaptable, allowing for extension to other BCC alloy systems and guiding high-throughput alloy design.

title: Pressure dependent DFT study of mechanical, thermal, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties of EuCd2As2: a magnetic semimetal
abstract: We present a comprehensive spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) investigation of the pressure-dependent physical properties of EuCd2As2, a magnetically and topologically rich compound with potential applications in spintronics and optoelectronics technologies. We have investigated the structural, mechanical, thermophysical, acoustic, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties of this material at pressures of 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 GPa. The calculated lattice parameters at zero pressure are in good agreement with experimental values. The mechanical stability of EuCd2As2 is maintained over the investigated pressure range. The elastic constants, bulk modulus, shear modulus, and Young's modulus are found to be tunable with applied pressure. The compound undergoes a brittle to ductile transition at higher pressures. The Debye temperature, melting temperature, and Grüneisen parameter are found to be strongly pressure-dependent. Phonon thermal conductivity has been evaluated. The electronic properties of EuCd2As2 were studied through band structure and density of states (DOS). The effect of pressure up to 8 GPa was investigated for the ferromagnetic (FM) phase. At 0 GPa, the calculated FM band structure exhibits no band gap at the Fermi level, which confirms the semimetallic nature of EuCd2As2. The net magnetic moment of 6.96 μ_B per unit cell was obtained for this compound indicating its potential for spintronics application. The optical properties, including the dielectric function, refractive index, absorption coefficient, optical conductivity, reflectivity, and loss function, are calculated. The calculated optical spectra indicate strong absorption in the visible and ultraviolet regions, suggesting that EuCd2As2 may have potential for optoelectronic applications.

title: Optimizing Drilling Trajectories in Multi-Material Structures Using Quantum Annealers
abstract: In this work we present a quantum-hybrid optimization approach for planning drilling trajectories on multi-material structures, with the objective of minimizing total energy consumption. The proposed formulation models the drilling process as a constrained routing problem in which each hole must be visited while accounting for heterogeneous material properties, material-dependent drilling costs and displacement energy, as well as tool-wear penalties. Our method incorporates realistic industrial constraints, including open-path routing and mandatory grouping of holes belonging to the same material to avoid frequent tool-bit changes. The modeled problem is solved using D-Wave's Leap Constrained Quadratic Model Hybrid Solver. To evaluate performance, we benchmark instances ranging from 10 to 55 holes with varying material distributions and cost matrices. The results highlight the capability of quantum-hybrid optimization to handle complex multi-physics constraints and to generate energy-efficient drilling sequences under realistic manufacturing conditions.

title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy
abstract: Understanding the onset of plastic deformation and the early development of strain localization is essential for characterizing material behavior and identifying failure-prone regions. However, these transitions are not always distinguishable from conventional full-field strain measurements. This study investigates a data- driven framework combining Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract temporal and spatial deformation signatures during uniaxial tensile loading. The methodology is evaluated using AA6063-T5 aluminum alloy specimens in the as-received condition and following thermal exposure at 100~$^\circ$C, 200~$^\circ$C, and 300~$^\circ$C. PCA applied to sequential strain fields reveals a characteristic peak in the second principal component projection near the yielding transition, showing agreement with the conventional 0.2\% offset criterion across the investigated conditions. Furthermore, principal component maps extracted from high-temporal-resolution strain fields preceding this transition highlight localized deformation features associated with subsequent failure regions. These features are more clearly distinguishable than competing strain concentrations in the corresponding instantaneous strain maps. The results indicate that PCA-derived deformation signatures remain identifiable despite thermally induced variations in mechanical response. This approach demonstrates the potential of unsupervised dimensionality reduction for extracting physically interpretable information on plastic deformation and early strain localization from experimental full-field measurements.

title: STAMP: Manufacturing-Informed Generative Design and Shape Optimization of Sheet Panels
abstract: Generative design of formed sheet panels must preserve geometric manufacturing conditions while exploring layouts and improving performance. STAMP embeds these conditions directly in the shape representation. Each panel is described by its material layout and a reference surface with one height at each occupied position in a plane perpendicular to the drawing direction. Nominal thickness is prescribed along the normal. The representation allows curved surfaces, ribs, and openings. It excludes reference-surface undercuts and keeps nominal thickness fixed without manufacturing penalty terms. Because these conditions belong to the representation, every generated and optimized panel satisfies them regardless of training-set size. Boundary-conditioned diffusion generates alternative layouts, and predictor gradients guide a surface optimization that retains outlines, openings, and designated fixed regions. We demonstrate STAMP on automotive hood inner panels using CarHoods10k. With a comparable number of stored values, depth maps reconstruct surfaces more accurately than point-cloud and voxel baselines. From only five training designs, one of three training runs yields novel and varied layouts. A generator trained on 500 designs, 6.5% of the training set, already reaches the layout variety of the full-data model. Across 11 held-out design families, predictor-based selection among existing dataset designs yields an average gap of 0.18 mm to the best available FEA deformation, versus an expected 1.59 mm for random selection. It does better than random selection in all 11 families. At a 10% depth-change bound, a network not used in the search predicts an average deformation reduction of 24.8% for six generated and existing panels, with a 3.2% average mass increase computed from geometry. Engineers can thus explore and optimize panels within this manufacturing-informed design space.

title: Large Language Model-Empowered Intelligent Agent for Adaptive Fast-Charging Control of Lithium-Ion Batteries
abstract: Fast charging of lithium-ion batteries is a multi-objective control problem that requires reducing charging time and sustaining high energy throughput while suppressing accelerated degradation and safety-critical electrochemical reactions. Conventional protocols are easy to implement but have limited ability to adapt to variations in battery chemistry, operating conditions, and aging state. Model-based optimization and conventional data-driven control often require accurate models, costly iterative search, or task-specific policies. We develop a large language model (LLM)-empowered intelligent agent for adaptive battery fast-charging control. In this closed-loop framework, the agent interprets structured battery states, generates executable charging actions, observes the resulting battery response, and continuously adjusts subsequent decisions. We construct a large-scale simulation corpus with PyBaMM across five battery chemistries and 11 parameter sets and convert the resulting state-action-response trajectories into structured process data for agent training. Our two-stage strategy combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). SFT establishes battery-control semantics and feasible decision priors from simulation-derived demonstrations. GRPO aligns the agent with a multi-objective control objective covering energy throughput, degradation mitigation, and operational constraints. Closed-loop simulations show that, under matched energy-throughput requirements, the agent achieves longer cycling life than conventional charging baselines and optimization-based strategies across heterogeneous battery configurations. This study provides a simulation-grounded proof of concept for using LLM agents as sequential decision makers in battery management and takes a step toward language-model-enabled control of physical energy systems.

title: Mapping the Phase Space of Cubic Chiral Semiconductors: High-Throughput Search,Stability, and Prototype Families
abstract: Chiral crystals show unique electronic, magnetic, and optical characteristics that make them attractive for topological and spintronic applications. Nevertheless, the limited set of identified chiral semiconductors, especially those with cubic symmetry, has so far constrained their technological application. In this work, we perform a high-throughput computational search for semiconducting chiral compounds in the cubic space group $P4_332$ (No. 212). By integrating machine-learning techniques with density functional theory, we obtain 24\,227 cubic chiral structures containing up to five elements, and identify 368 thermodynamically stable semiconductors on the convex hull and 3\,048 within 50~meV/atom. We analyze their structural motifs, stability, and electronic band structures, highlighting recurring prototype families, several of which show intrinsic intermediate-band features. Our results substantially expand the known phase space of cubic chiral semiconductors and may guide future efforts in the discovery and design of chiral materials.

title: On the Limits of Sufficient Explanations
abstract: We formally characterize the conditions under which sufficient explanations exist for classifiers on structured data such as graphs and strings. We focus on post-hoc explainers that select parts of the input as sufficient explanations. An explanation is sufficient if the selected part alone ensures the predicted label. Sufficient explanations have been widely adopted across data modalities, including graphs, strings, and images. However, a unified formal analysis of sufficient explanations remains missing. We bridge this gap with four main contributions: (i) We define a general explanation formalism consisting of an instance space, a classifier, and a select relation. The select relation specifies which potential sub-instances or feature subsets can be selected as explanations from each instance; (ii) We show that the existence of sufficient explainers is fully characterized by the interplay between the classifier and the select relation; (iii) We extend this analysis to practically relevant variants of sufficiency, including probabilistic sufficiency and deletion sufficiency; (iv) Based on the formal analysis, we devise statistics that bound the maximum achievable sufficiency for a given task. We evaluate these statistics on language, protein, and molecular classification datasets and find that full sufficiency is unattainable on most of them. Since these bounds hold for every explainer, they provide a task-level reference against which any explainer's sufficiency can be judged in absolute terms.

title: Tunable coupling between valley and magnetic excitons in WS2/CrSBr heterostructures
abstract: Interfacial coupling in van der Waals two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures offers an effective route to tailor the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of materials. Versatile control and precise engineering of such interlayer interactions can be further achieved through external parameters, like electric field, magnetic field, optical excitation, as well as layer stacking geometries. Here, we examined the magneto-optical properties of 2D semiconductor heterostructures made of antiferromagnetic CrSBr and a monolayer WS2, both of which host intriguing excitonic properties. We identified a type-II band alignment between these two layers and the magnetic proximity effects from CrSBr, manifested by an enhanced Zeeman valley splitting in the WS2 layer. The interlayer charge transfer shows strong spin selectivity and is governed by the relative alignment between the valley-spin polarization of photoexcited carriers in WS2 and the magnetization in CrSBr, giving rise to spin-sensitive circularly polarized photoluminescence (PL) from WS2. Furthermore, the highly anisotropic electronic dispersion in CrSBr enables stacking-dependent control of interlayer interactions, as inferred from a twist-angle dependence of PL quenching. Our work establishes a highly tunable 2D system that integrates valleytronics and magnetic excitons through multiple coupling channels, opening up new opportunities in all-optical manipulation of spin and magnon states and for the development of flexible spin-optoelectronic devices.

title: Critical Assessments of Computational Hit-finding Experiments Challenge #4: Targeting the Tyrosine Kinase Binding Domain of the E3 Ligase Casitas B-Lineage Lymphoma Proto-Oncogene B, an Immuno-Oncology Target
abstract: The critical assessments of computational hit-finding experiments (CACHE) are prospective benchmarking exercises where small molecule ligands predicted for a nominated protein of interest are procured and tested experimentally. In CACHE #4, 23 participating teams each selected up to 100 compounds designed to bind the E3 ligase CBLB, an immuno-oncology target. The organizers released the first public structure of CBLB in complex with a known ligand at the outset of the challenge to enable the discovery of chemically novel molecules.
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: Genome-scale mining and experimental characterization of antimicrobial peptides from Bacillus
abstract: The escalating global crisis of antibiotic resistance necessitates the development of novel antibacterial agents. The genus Bacillus, a prolific producer of bioactive secondary metabolites, represents an important resource for the discovery of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs). In this study, we integrated large-scale genomic analysis with machine learning to systematically mine 3,283 high-quality Bacillus genomes from the NCBI database. A total of 6,532 putative AMP sequences were identified and clustered into 682 antimicrobial peptide cluster families (ACFs).

title: The deep learning framework Hist2Prot infers single-cell spatial proteomics from histology to predict biomarkers and clinical outcomes
abstract: Spatial proteomics enables high-resolution mapping of protein expression within the tumor microenvironment, but its routine clinical application remains limited by cost, technical complexity and restricted tissue coverage. Here we present Hist2Prot, a deep learning framework that generates single-cell spatial proteomic profiles from routine hematoxylin and eosin histology.

title: Molecular sensor makes invisible traces of mercury easier to see
abstract: Mercury contamination presents an obvious challenge: it is invisible. A glass of water or a piece of fruit can seem perfectly normal to the naked eye, even when trace amounts of toxic mercury are present. Detecting such minute levels usually requires specialized laboratory tools and trained experts.

title: High-Performance All-Atom Continuous Constant-pH Molecular Dynamics and Native Asynchronous Replica Exchange in Amber
abstract: Conformational dynamics of biomolecules, including proteins and nucleic acids, are often coupled to changes in protonation states. All-atom particle-mesh Ewald continuous constant-pH molecular dynamics (PME-CpHMD) enables proton-coupled dynamics, but its routine use has been limited by computational cost. Here we report a second-generation CUDA implementation of PME-CpHMD in Amber, in which the CpHMD-specific nonbonded corrections are evaluated in a separate kernel. Across protein systems ranging from 45 to 1,338 residues, the new implementation increases throughput by 1.5-2 fold relative to the previous fused-kernel implementation and limits the overhead relative to conventional MD to 12-18%. We also implemented the asynchronous pH replica-exchange (pH-REX) algorithm natively in pmemd.cuda.MPI, allowing simulations to run on fewer GPUs than replicas without the overhead of the previous Python wrapper. Furthermore, we derived CpHMD titration parameters for all six titratable residue types (Asp, Glu, His, Cys, Tyr, and Lys) for use with three protein force fields: CHARMM c22/CMAP, Amber ff14sb and ff19sb. The new implementations and parameterization were validated using pKa calculations of model peptides and hen egg white lysozyme (HEWL). The HEWL simulations revealed force-field-specific limitations, including overestimation of the pKa downshift 20 of H15 and sensitivity of the proton donor assignment in coupled E35/D52 dyad. Comparison with our previous work and the PME-CpHMD simulations in GROMACS with the CHARMM c36m force field demonstrated the robustness and sampling efficiency of pH-REX PME-CpHMD simulations. The new implementation provides a foundation for routine all-atom constant-pH simulations in Amber. The analysis highlights the need for continued development of protein force fields to more accurately balance intramolecular electrostatics and solvation of charged residues.

title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
abstract: Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature. The breakthrough has already revealed promising new quantum building blocks that could help unlock computing capabilities far beyond those of today's supercomputers.

title: Multimodal Fusion: A Review of Breast Cancer Advanced and Traditional Modalities
abstract: Purpose: Multimodal medical imaging fusion (MMIF) is an increasingly important approach to breast cancer detection (BCD), as different imaging modalities rely on different physical principles and provide complementary information. No single modality can capture all the structural, functional, and biological information needed for accurate diagnosis and characterization. Methods: This review examines more than 15 imaging modalities used in breast cancer detection, including conventional techniques such as mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), as well as emerging approaches such as thermal imaging, photoacoustic imaging, microwave imaging, and multimodal microscopy. Results: Mammography, ultrasound, and MRI remain among the most widely used modalities, providing complementary structural and functional information. Recent AI advances have enabled fusion at the data, feature, and decision levels, with applications in detection, classification, segmentation, prognosis, and personalized cancer management. Multimodal approaches increasingly combine imaging data with clinical, histopathological, and genomic information. However, important challenges remain, including limited availability of large and diverse multimodal datasets, variations in imaging protocols, missing modalities, limited external validation, and the need for interpretable and clinically reliable AI models. Conclusion: MMIF offers promising opportunities to improve breast cancer detection and characterization by combining complementary imaging and non-imaging information. Future research should prioritize robust fusion strategies, standardized and diverse datasets, multicenter validation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, and the integration of imaging with clinical and molecular data to facilitate reliable translation into clinical practice.

title: A Practitioner's Guide to Materials Theory and Computation in the Age of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Computational modelling has become a cornerstone of materials science, with advances in atomistic simulations, high-throughput computation, and artificial intelligence transforming how materials are understood, discovered, and designed. These developments build upon generations of theoretical innovations that have translated complex mathematical and physical principles into practical predictive tools. However, the growing diversity of computational methods presents challenges for practitioners seeking a coherent understanding of their theoretical foundations. Drawing upon the author's research experience, this monograph provides a practitioner-oriented, pedagogical overview of computational materials science, unified through the concepts of potential-energy landscapes and statistical sampling. It explores how these concepts underpin structural stability, phase behaviour, and electronic and magnetic properties, through a systematic treatment of empirical force fields, density-functional theory, many-body electronic-structure methods, statistical sampling, and property prediction. It further examines high-throughput workflows, materials databases, and the probabilistic foundations of artificial intelligence. Particular emphasis is placed on atomistic representations, graph neural networks, and generative models, highlighting the roles of symmetry, group theory, differential geometry, and stochastic processes in modern materials modelling. By connecting established physical theories with emerging data-driven approaches, this monograph offers a unified perspective on computational materials science and identifies opportunities and challenges toward physics-informed, efficient, and reliable materials discovery.

title: Lower Bound of Thermal Conductivity in Graphene
abstract: The intrinsic thermal conductivity ($κ$) of graphene remains highly controversial because of physical and metrological complexities. Although the thermal bridge method enables reliable measurements, sample fabrication remains challenging. Here, we develop a highly efficient patterning and transfer technique to systematically fabricate and characterize suspended bilayer graphene (BLG) thermal bridges with lengths of 1-30 $μ$m. Suspended BLG with unavoidable polymer residues exhibits length-independent thermal conductivity of approximately 570 W/(m K) at room temperature, remaining nearly constant from 250 to 350 K and robust to rigorous surface cleaning and amorphous silicon nitride substrates. Homogeneous non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (HNEMD) simulations show that amorphous carbon coverage of only approximately 0.01 monolayer is sufficient to suppress out-of-plane flexural acoustic (ZA) phonons. These findings challenge the prevailing view that rigid substrates suppress ZA phonons more strongly than surface contamination and identify a robust lower bound of $κ$ governed by amorphous surface scattering. This lower bound reflects heat conduction in graphene under realistic device conditions and provides a reference for fundamental phonon transport studies and the integration of graphene into thermal management applications in electronic devices and chips.

title: Chromosome-level genomics and cross-species enzyme screening enable high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica
abstract: The diversity of enzymes supporting bakuchiol biosynthesis remains incompletely characterized, limiting the repertoire available for microbial pathway engineering. Here, we combined chromosome-level genomics, cross-species enzyme screening and metabolic engineering to establish high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica. We assembled a 471.76-Mb Psoralea corylifolia genome anchored to 11 pseudochromosomes, with a contig N50 of 40.33 Mb. Genome-guided screening and functional validation identified four prenyltransferases from P. corylifolia and Vigna radiata whose N-terminally truncated variants supported bakuchiol production in yeast. These results extend experimental evidence for bakuchiol-producing activity across legume prenyltransferase sequences and species. For PcPT6, corresponding to the previously reported PcPT07, removing 40 N-terminal amino acids increased bakuchiol production by 53% relative to the full-length enzyme. We reconstructed bakuchiol biosynthesis in Y. lipolytica and reinforced aromatic precursor synthesis to increase p-coumaric acid supply. Coordinating mevalonate pathway reinforcement with increased t40PcPT6 gene dosage further improved bakuchiol production. Following fermentation optimization, titers reached 108.29 mg/L in shake flasks and 6.03 g/L in a 7.5-L fed-batch bioreactor. These findings connect an expanded set of functional prenyltransferases with coordinated pathway engineering, enabling gram-per-liter microbial bakuchiol production.

title: Expanding Plasma Proteome Coverage While Preserving Biological Signatures: A Systematic Characterization of Enrichment and Preanalytical Variables
abstract: Plasma is a rich and accessible source for biomarkers. The analytical challenge of the steep dynamic range was recently addressed using enrichment technologies. Enrichment technologies have been shown to be sensitive to preanalytical variables, making this an active area of research. We established the P2 enrichment system as high-performing and robust for large scale studies, with reproducible identifications and precision across batches, days, operators and laboratories. We characterized P2-based enrichment for preanalytical variables (eight blood collection types, centrifugation, freeze-thaw and pathogen inactivation). K2EDTA-plasma resulted in the deepest proteome coverage with about 6000 protein groups on the timsTOF HT. We spiked 16 heavy-labelled proteins into platelet-poor and platelet-contaminated plasma. Importantly, linearity, accuracy, and precision were high in both platelet-poor and platelet-contaminated plasma for both P2-enriched and neat preparations. In a cancer cohort, we demonstrated that 97% of differentially abundant proteins retained the same direction of regulation after P2-based enrichment compared with the neat preparation. Differentially abundant proteins identified in a colorectal cancer pilot cohort remained largely conserved after platelet contamination, including previously reported biomarkers. We demonstrated that P2-based enrichment enables deep, large scale proteome profiling and preserves biological information despite preanalytical variation. Candidates emerging from P2-based discovery can be validated in independent cohorts with targeted assays.

title: Lipid Scrambling Amplifies Plasma Membrane Undulations via Anti-Registered Domains Stabilized by Long-Chain Sphingomyelin
abstract: Lipid scrambling, which dissipates the transbilayer lipid asymmetry of plasma membranes (PMs), plays an essential role in various large-scale membrane remodeling processes. Although lipid domains have been implicated in these processes, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, owing to the lack of a molecular-level picture of how lipid scrambling reorganizes these domains. Here, using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of asymmetric and fully scrambled PM models, we show that lipid scrambling markedly enhances membrane undulations. We identify two key features of the domain organization underlying this enhancement in the scrambled PM: domain anti-registration, which couples to membrane curvature through a mismatch in preferred curvature between the two leaflets, and scrambling-induced domain enlargement, which permits this curvature to extend over large length scales. Simulations with different sphingomyelin (SM) compositions demonstrate that long-chain SMs stabilize anti-registered domains and the associated membrane curvature. Together, these results suggest a physical mechanism by which lipid scrambling primes the PM for remodeling through the reorganization of lipid domains, with long-chain SMs playing a key role. We also find that the interleaflet domain organization of the scrambled PM model depends strongly on system size, shifting from anti-registration to registration as the simulation box is reduced, and we discuss the origin of this finite-size effect.

title: Optimizing assay conditions for gaussia luciferase
abstract: Gaussia luciferase (GLuc) is a widely used reporter enzyme due to its small size and exceptionally intense light output. However, its characteristic 'flash' properties have made accurate determination of enzyme activity sensitive to minute variations in the experimental setup, which is the likely cause of many inconsistent and contradictory findings in the literature. The intrinsic instability of the substrate, coelenterazine, adds to these complications. Furthermore, at the high dilutions commonly required to measure this exceptionally active enzyme, the signal often deviates from the expected linear relationship between activity and concentration due to adsorption. In this study, we systematically investigated the critical experimental parameters that affect activity measurements using a 96-well plate reader with an automated injection system. To illustrate experimental issues, we applied our analysis to measurements of GLuc and GLuc variants with widely different levels of activity and decay rates as well as with different substrates. We demonstrate that variations in 1) latency between substrate injection and measurement, 2) enzyme dilution and adhesion, and 3) substrate handling and degradation can lead to inconsistent values for specific activity. Based on this, we suggest a framework for optimizing GLuc assay conditions for reproducibility.

title: Evaluating speech-like distortion product otoacoustic emissions: a comparison of time- and frequency-domain metrics across three datasets
abstract: Speech-like distortion-product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs) allow cochlear activity to be measured during the perception of natural, continuous speech and have been used to study attentional effects in the cochlea. The technique is still young, however, and existing studies differ in stimulus design and in the metric used to quantify the emissions, which makes their results difficult to compare. Here, we reanalysed three existing datasets (106 participants, 14 stimulus types) with a common pipeline. We compared six metrics: the band power of the recording, the magnitude-squared coherence (MSC) between the recording and a DPOAE template, and four metrics derived from their complex cross-correlation, namely peak magnitude, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), peak area and peak width. A separability index quantified how well each metric separated in-ear recordings from out-of-ear control recordings without emissions. Band power, MSC and SNR separated best, with mean separability indices of about 0.9, whereas the peak magnitude performed worst and was inverted for half of the stimulus types. Since band power does not require a DPOAE template, it serves as a sanity check of the setup rather than as evidence for an emission. The MSC was insensitive to the latency of the emission but well suited for comparisons across stimuli, whereas the cross-correlation additionally provided the latency. The emissions differed significantly between the stimulus types of the three datasets, and those below about 700 Hz were measured least reliably. We derive practical recommendations for the analysis and stimulus design of future experiments.

title: Advancing AOPs for genotoxicity through quantifying KERs linking DNA alkylation to increase in mutations and chromosome aberrations
abstract: Quantitative Adverse Outcome Pathways (qAOPs) help translate mechanistic knowledge into quantitative toxicity predictions; however, their development is constrained by the limited availability and heterogeneity of quantitative data. Here, we investigated the feasibility of developing a qAOP for genotoxicity by modeling quantitative relationships linking DNA alkylation to increased mutations and structural chromosome aberrations through intermediate biological key events (KEs). We compiled and harmonized published concentration-response data from human lymphoblastoid TK6 cells exposed to ethyl methanesulfonate, methyl methanesulfonate, or N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea, covering eight genotoxicity assays representing five KEs with well-established dependencies. We evaluated sources of variability, compared points of departure (PoDs), and quantified relationships between successive events using response-response modeling. Substantial between-study variability could to a limited extent be explained through differences in experimental design while batch effects for individual studies and researchers were substantial. PoD estimates that were calculated from combined results of independent studies with similar experimental design, were often uncertain due to insufficient concentration-response characterization or conflicting results between studies. Nevertheless, response-response modeling suggested a threshold effect for certain key-event relationships (KERs). Specifically, DNA adducts seemed to be triggered at lower concentrations of alkylating agents compared to the subsequent KEs of DNA strand breaks and chromosome aberrations. Furthermore, these fitted response-response models can be used for prediction of downstream KEs from earlier ones. The general approach we developed for BMC analysis followed by response-response modeling is applicable to other AOPs as well. These findings highlight both the feasibility and limitations of using existing data for qAOP development.

title: Combining KA Oil Oxidation and O2 Reduction to H2O2 Enables Kinetically and Energetically Favored Adipic Acid Production Pathways
abstract: Adipic acid (AA), produced via oxidation of KA oil (a mixture of cyclohexanol and cyclohexanone), is a crucial monomer for nylon-6,6 synthesis. Electrochemical oxidation of KA oil eliminates the use of the nitric acid oxidant in the conventional process, offering a greener approach. However, electrochemical KA oil oxidation is slow; in particular, the 6e– oxidation of cyclohexanone to AA is sluggish, increasing electrical energy consumption. Here, we demonstrate that pairing KA oil oxidation with the 2e– oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) mitigates energetic and kinetic limitations. By replacing the commonly used hydrogen evolution reaction with the ORR, the operating voltage is greatly reduced. More importantly, we discovered that H2O2 generated from the 2e– ORR can oxidize cyclohexanone to 6-hydroperoxyhexanoic acid (HPHA), a reaction not previously reported in the literature. HPHA can then be further electrochemically oxidized to AA with significantly faster kinetics than cyclohexanone, effectively eliminating the kinetic bottleneck of electrochemical cyclohexanone oxidation. This discovery enables a three-step pathway for AA production: electrochemical oxidation of cyclohexanol to cyclohexanone, chemical oxidation of cyclohexanone to HPHA by H2O2, and electrochemical oxidation of HPHA to AA. The selectivity and efficiency of each reaction, as well as those of the overall process, are investigated in detail.

title: Fine-tuned atomistic foundation model for accurate sodium-carbon chemistry in Na-ion batteries
abstract: Atomistic foundation models have emerged as a promising route to DFT-level accuracy for materials simulation with complex chemical environments. However, their reliability across competing bonding regimes and, more importantly, how complex bonding affects predictions of material properties remain unclear. Among materials with competing bonding regimes, sodium storage in hard carbon poses a substantial challenge. Hard carbon features diverse local structural motifs, including defective and curved graphitic regions, amorphous regions, and closed/open pores. Motivated by its importance for Na-ion batteries, we systematically evaluate existing pretrained foundation models based on the MACE architecture across different local Na/C motifs. We find that the pretrained models fail to accurately capture Na-Na and Na-C interactions for metallic Na clusters on graphene. To recover a DFT-level energetic description, we employ targeted fine-tuning, showing that it can describe the energetic stability of local motifs and achieve sufficient transferability to unseen Na/C environments. With the developed fine-tuned model, we establish a correlation between closed-pore radius in hard carbon and plateau voltage, showing that the small pores contribute at larger voltages than large ones, suggesting thus how the developed fine-tuned foundation model can link atomistic information with materials design for complex bonding environments.

title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures
abstract: Atomic disorder offers a potent degree of freedom to tailor material properties, yet the resulting vast configuration space obscures structure-property relations and hinders rational inverse design. Here we introduce Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (GaDiT), a generative model that combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution. GaDiT generates high-quality disordered structures while accelerating sampling by two orders of magnitude compared with existing corrector-based approaches, as demonstrated across two-dimensional amorphous carbon and three-dimensional amorphous silicon and silica. Moreover, GaDiT supports conditional generation under single or combined structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions in a unified model, and enables inverse design that expands accessible structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. To interpret these structures and the trained network, we propose a conditioned atomic response mapping analysis, revealing both the global structural descriptors and the local atomic environments that govern target properties. Overall, GaDiT establishes a general framework for interpretable generation, inverse design and structure-property discovery for disordered atomic structures.

title: High Entropy Oxides as Room Temperature Anderson Insulators with Colossal Soft Gaps
abstract: The Anderson effect, arising from destructive quantum interference of electron wave packets in disordered potentials, is usually observed at cryogenic temperatures and typically arises from extrinsic defects in conventional materials such as phosphorus dopants in silicon or oxygen vacancies in transition metal oxides. Here we demonstrate that a multication lattice of transition metals in a high-entropy oxide (HEO) natively establishes an interacting Anderson insulator that extends up to $500\,\mathrm{K}$. By controlling the population of transition metal cations in $\mathrm{La}_{0.7}\mathrm{Sr}_{0.3}\mathrm{Mn}_{1-x}(\mathrm{Cr},\mathrm{Fe},\mathrm{Co},\mathrm{Ni})_{x/4}\mathrm{O}_3$ (LS5B), we tune the system from the prototypical correlated metal $\mathrm{La}_{0.7}\mathrm{Sr}_{0.3}\mathrm{Mn}\mathrm{O}_3$ at $x=0.00$ to a localized insulator at $x=0.80$, where the disorder length contracts to near the unit cell (3.85 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$) and drives the electron mean free path to the Ioffe-Regel limit. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) reveals the systematic localization of itinerant $d$-quasiparticle states at the Fermi level, consistent with the emergence of a soft Coulomb gap, while the underlying band structure and symmetry are preserved. Transport reveals Efros-Shklovskii variable-range hopping governed by a colossal soft gap with characteristic temperature $T_{\mathrm{ES}}>50{,}000\,\mathrm{K}$ and screened Coulomb interaction strengths as high as 1.6 eV. Together, multiple lines of evidence indicate that interacting Anderson behavior is a native characteristic that survives to temperatures as high as $500\,\mathrm{K}$ in high-entropy materials.

title: Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) show promise for predicting materials properties, but interpretability remains a challenge, particularly understanding whether attributed feature importance reflects physical reality or statistical artifacts. Here, we present a methods validation study that deliberately overfits a physics-aware GNN ensemble to probe the robustness of feature-ranking approaches. Using the CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy system with three stoichiometries, we train GNNs to predict decomposition enthalpies from DFT-calculated structures while explicitly constraining output weights to encode feature importance. By design, our dataset is limited (approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways) to control compositional complexity and enable precise interrogation of local chemistry effects. We validate that feature rankings capture meaningful local-environment information through a series of atomic swap perturbations: perturbing individual atomic sites and re-ranking features reveals spatial decay consistent with the GNN's interaction cutoff, confirming that weights encode neighbor-shell effects rather than global stoichiometric artifacts alone. Results demonstrate that feature attribution methods can remain physically interpretable even under overfitting, provided validation is rigorous. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy interpretability in materials GNNs and sets the stage for scaling to multiple chemistries and testing generalization across compositional spaces.

title: Uniaxial strain induces $d$-wave phonon chirality in ferroelectric BaTiO$_3$
abstract: Circularly dichroic resonant inelastic x-ray scattering has revealed electrically switchable $g$-wave phonon chirality in freestanding BaTiO$_3$ membranes. Here, we show from first principles that uniaxial strain changes the angular class of this texture. Lowering $C_{4v}$ to $C_{2v}$ adds a $d$-wave helicity that is bilinear in the orthorhombic strain $η$ and the polarization, with nodal lines along the stress axis. For the 38~meV branches at $η=1\%$, we find that (i) along the diagonal, where the helicity vanishes by symmetry without strain, it reaches about 60\% of the unstrained maximum, and (ii) at the measured wave vectors off the mirror it is reduced by more than half. With PBEsol and PBE+D3 force constants, the $d$-wave component grows linearly in $η$ and equals the $g$-wave one at $η^*\approx1.3\text{--}1.4\%$. Resolved by branch, the response of strain-split $E$ doublets is non-analytic in $η$, as captured by a two-band model. Strain therefore provides a second knob, besides the electric field, that controls the symmetry and the sign of phonon chirality in ferroelectric membranes.

title: Score-based neural ordinary differential equations for reaction-diffusions
abstract: A diffusion equation can be rewritten as a transport equation driven by the score function of the evolving density. Conventional probability-flow formulations, which move particles deterministically with this score-driven velocity, typically conserve total mass. In this work, we develop a Lagrangian method for reaction-diffusion equations in which each particle carries a position and a physical weight. The characteristic ODEs incorporate source terms into the evolution of the log-density and its gradient, while particle weights track changes in mass. We combine this representation with a learned velocity field and weighted particle training to approximate these dynamics. For non-increasing reaction rates, a relative-entropy inequality supports the mass-normalized self-consistency residual as the training objective. This objective can control the error of the induced density when the growth rate is bounded. The algorithm divides the time interval into short windows. In each window, a frozen velocity generates the particle data for a regression of the network velocity. We draw the particles from period-adapted initial sampling distributions and weight them in the loss partly by their predicted future mass, because the reaction can make regions with little initial mass important later. We numerically investigate the method on the Ornstein--Uhlenbeck (OU) equation with a linear source term, Fisher--KPP equations, and Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao gradient flows.

title: Machine learning of strength surfaces enables high regularization length phase-field fracture
abstract: Classical phase-field models of brittle fracture capture toughness-controlled crack growth but not the material's strength surface, which governs crack nucleation. The theory of Kumar et al. (2020) incorporates the strength surface through a nucleation driving force, and Chockalingam (2025) derived this driving force for arbitrary strength surfaces described by $n$ material parameters, with which the phase-field strength surface (PFSS) converges to the material strength surface as the regularization length $\varepsilon \to 0$ and matches it exactly at $n$ chosen states for any $\varepsilon$. In practice, however, the strength surface must be supplied as an analytic form chosen and calibrated case by case, and for the widely used analytic surfaces ($n=2$) accurate strength reproduction requires $\varepsilon$ commensurate with the Irwin characteristic length $l_{ch}$, imposing prohibitive mesh requirements for large structures. We introduce a neural-network (NN) strength function that is learned directly from strength data, is physics-constrained by construction, and provides far more calibration parameters than analytic surfaces; the calibration is generalized to any number of strength states and to enforce openness in chosen directions. A single architecture captures synthetic data from the Mohr-Coulomb, Drucker-Prager, Mogi-Coulomb and 3D Hoek-Brown surfaces and experimental data for graphite, natural rubber and styrene-butadiene rubber. The resulting PFSS is accurate up to $\varepsilon = 10\,l_{ch}$, whereas that of the exact analytic surfaces performs comparatively poorly even at $\varepsilon = 0.5\,l_{ch}$. Finite-element simulations validate the theory across fracture regimes. By decoupling strength fidelity from the regularization length, the approach substantially reduces the mesh resolution required for phase-field fracture simulations of large structures.

title: Spin Exchange Enables Two-Electron TEMPO Catholytes for Aqueous Organic Flow Batteries
abstract: High-energy-density neutral aqueous organic redox flow batteries (AORFBs) require a transition from one-electron/one-electron and two-electron/one-electron configurations to fully two-electron-matched systems. This goal has remained unrealized because stable two-electron catholytes are lacking, and even the most promising TEMPO materials still undergo proton-induced irreversible piperidine ring opening, causing rapid capacity decay. Here we report a hydration-cage-induced spin-exchange strategy for stabilizing two-electron AcNH-NMe-TEMPO catholytes.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: A reversible YbbR-domain hinge switch senses extracellular pH to control bacterial cyclic-di-AMP signaling
abstract: Acidification is a principal antimicrobial host defence: during infection, bacteria have to survive the stomach, the vaginal tract or the phagolysosome of immune cells, where the pH falls below 5. To persist, bacteria must sense and adapt to extracellular pH. In Gram-positive bacteria, the membrane protein CdaR, a regulator of the c-di-AMP-synthesizing enzyme CdaA, has been proposed as a pH sensor, but the molecular basis of this sensing remains unknown. Here we show, using the model organism Bacillus subtilis, that CdaR is essential for growth below pH 5.

title: Overlap of competing voices may mask attentional effects on speech-like distortion product otoacoustic emissions
abstract: Whether selective auditory attention modulates the cochlear amplifier through the medial olivocochlear system remains debated. Using speech-like distortion-product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs), elicited by waveforms that follow the harmonics of natural speech, we previously found that selectively attending one of two competing talkers reduced the emissions related to the resolved harmonics of the female voice. Here, we attempted to reproduce this effect in a design that separated different frequency regimes and harmonic resolvability. Forty-four participants attended one of two competing talkers, a female and a male voice, presented to one ear, while speech-like DPOAEs related to both voices were recorded from the other ear. Stimuli were derived from resolved and unresolved harmonics in a low-frequency (up to 1.5 kHz) and a transitional (1.5 to 4 kHz) regime, which required pitch-shifting both voices so that their fundamental frequencies were much closer to each other than in the original study. Speech-like DPOAEs emerged for most stimulus types, although they were weak for some and absent for one. Their amplitude, however, did not depend on attention for any stimulus type. Further time-domain metrics showed only isolated attentional effects of opposite direction for two stimulus types, and a frequency-domain metric showed none. A cochlear excitation model suggests that, due to the closely spaced fundamental frequencies of the two voices, the emissions most comparable to the original study presumably arose at cochlear locations shared by both voices, where attention would modulate both voices alike.

title: Actin Assembly on Biomimetic Lipid-coated and Functionalized Bead Surfaces
abstract: Dynamic assembly of actin filaments drives cell protrusion and other aspects of cell motility. Reconstitution of actin assembly from purified components is a powerful approach for understanding the molecular mechanisms that underlie these processes. Purified preparations of actin, actin-binding proteins, and regulators of actin-binding proteins enable a broad spectrum of reconstitution experiments. Much of this actin filament assembly occurs at the plasma membrane, with exquisite temporal and spatial regulation. We developed a biomimetic reconstitution system using purified lipids or glutathione on the surface of functionalized beads as models for actin assembly at the plasma membrane. The system incorporates two critical pathways for regulation of actin assembly: nucleation of actin polymerization by Arp2/3 complex and activation of heterodimeric actin capping protein (CP). Arp2/3 complex and CP are both essentially inactive in the basal resting state of the cytoplasm. The system incorporates membrane-bound activators for Arp2/3 complex, such as WASP and WAVE family proteins, and for CP, such as CARMILs and other CPI-motif proteins. Membrane-bound components are coupled to beads either through lipids, which allow lateral mobility, or through glutathione groups attached to the bead surface via flexible linkers. Fluorescence microscopy of labeled components, combined with quantitative image analysis, is used to assess the combined effects of the regulators and thereby test molecular mechanisms for regulation of actin assembly. Here, we describe protocols for preparing functionalized beads, coupling regulators to the bead surface, performing actin assembly reactions, and imaging and quantifying the resulting actin networks.

title: Binary Patterning as a Probe of Protein Language Model Representations
abstract: Do protein language models (pLMs) encode the physical rules that govern protein folding? The four-helix bundle provides a classic test case because binary patterning, the ordered placement of polar and nonpolar residues along an amphipathic -helix, is sufficient to generate folded proteins with high probability. Here, we ask whether ESM2 captures the sequence grammar underlying this design strategy. Libraries of synthetic sequences constrained only by binary patterning were predicted by ESMFold to form four-helix bundles. Predicted helicity, compactness, and topological diversity changed with sequence length in the same direction as experimentally characterized libraries, although the model did not distinguish successful from unsuccessful individual designs. Principal component analysis of ESM2 embeddings revealed representations of hydrophobic patterning, helix-loop boundaries, and heptad register. Extending the analysis to all 128 heptad binary patterns produced a jellyfish-shaped manifold in which hydrophobic composition formed the dominant axis, while paired components encoded pattern phase. Manifold geometry depended on amino-acid chemistry, repeat number, and linker sequence, and collapsed when amino acids were assigned to arbitrary categories. ESM2 therefore combines general repeat recognition with protein-specific physicochemical information. More broadly, synthetic sequence libraries provide experimentally grounded probes of protein language model representations and their relationship to protein biophysics.

title: Cochlear wave dispersion reveals partition micromechanics
abstract: Cochlear traveling waves are a fundamental aspect of mammalian hearing, enabling frequency selectivity. However, incorporating micromechanical interactions between the cells, membranes, and fluids that comprise the cochlear partition presents a challenge when accounting for this selectivity and other macro-scale response properties. The traveling wave can be characterized by its dispersion, which is the relationship between its wavenumber and frequency. One objective was to investigate how organ of Corti structural components influence wave dispersion. To achieve this, we adapted a conventional three-dimensional tapered cochlear box model by incrementally adding morphological characteristics that constitute the partition. Initially a flexible plate, the partition transformed to incorporate a tectorial membrane and inner spiral sulcus. Our secondary objective was to predict the dispersion for each variation using a reduced-length model (slice model). We observed that stiffness and the optimal frequency increased across variations, while wave dispersion remained unchanged relative to the optimal frequency. We also discovered that eigenfrequency analysis, using Floquet boundary conditions, accurately predicted the dispersion for each variation and revealed the existence of other propagating waves including a tectorial membrane transverse mode. These results underscore the significance of analyzing cochlear wave propagation from capturing macromechanical response properties thereby facilitating investigations of micromechanical interactions in reduced-length models.

title: Multiscale Drug–Cell Interaction Modeling via Hybrid Graph Architectures and Knowledge-Aware Fusion for Drug Synergy Prediction
abstract: Accurate prediction of drug combination synergy remains challenging due to the vast combinatorial space and strong cellular context dependency of drug responses. To address these limitations, we present MILSyn, a multimodal interaction learning framework designed to capture multiscale drug–cell interactions through three integrated components: (1) relational modeling of heterogeneous graph structures using a hybrid RGCN-GATv2 architecture, (2) cross-modal fusion of biochemical features spanning SMILES, substructures, 3D conformations, and multiomic profiles, and (3) knowledge-aware reasoning…
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: Two-Step Photon Absorption in an Expanded Perovskite Analog with a Molecular Intermediate Band
abstract: Intermediate-band solar cells (IBSCs) introduce an intermediate band (IB) within the absorber’s band gap, allowing consecutive sub-band-gap two-step photon absorption (TSPA) to supplement band-gap absorption, enabling a 50% increase in the fundamental device efficiency limit. Current IBSC absorbers, however, introduce the IB as impurities in trace concentrations, affording weak sub-band-gap absorption. We demonstrate a novel material design for TSPA using (dmpz)Pb2I6 (dmpz2+ = N,N′-dimethylpyrazinium) containing a molecular IB. Notably, the organic–inorganic hybridization evident in electronic structure calculations, where electronic states from the iodide appear in the dmpz-based bands, and large thermal fluctuations revealed by molecular dynamics trajectories enhance subgap absorption at 300 K. Transient electronic signatures of photoreduced dmpz•+ radicals verify the charge-transfer nature of the sub-band-gap absorption, whereas coherent high-frequency vibrations reveal vibronic coupling between dmpz and the inorganic framework. Proof-of-concept solar cells with (dmpz)Pb2I6 generate increased photocurrent upon subgap IR excitation and display quadratic-to-linear power dependence. This first demonstration of TSPA with an intrinsic organic IB offers a new material class for IBSCs.

title: Solution of the Qubit Marginal Problem from Fermionic Representability
abstract: Whether local reduced states are compatible with a global quantum state---the quantum marginal problem---is central to quantum information and simulation. Here we present a solution to the ensemble marginal problem for qubits based on the representability theory of fermions. Encoding each qubit as one fermion in two orbitals, we prove that the representable qubit marginals form an exposed face of the set of $N$-representable fermionic reduced density matrices, selected by the vanishing of every site-occupation variance. Complete hierarchies of fermionic representability conditions therefore transfer exactly to qubits. Applications to frustrated Heisenberg and transverse-field Ising rings show that the $(2,3)$-positivity conditions are exact at the Majumdar--Ghosh point and accurate to about 0.5% at criticality. Because the conditions hold for any quantum state, they also provide a framework for mitigating measurement errors on qubit-based quantum devices.

title: Pressure and Magnetic Field Control of Topology in Antiferromagnetic Bilayers
abstract: Controlling band topology in magnetic semiconductors requires strategies that couple electronic structure to experimentally accessible degrees of freedom. Here we propose a cooperative approach based on pressure and magnetic reorientation in A-type antiferromagnetic bilayers. Antiparallel layer magnetizations suppress hybridization between exchange-polarized band-edge states, limiting their response to interlayer compression. A magnetic field that aligns the layer moments removes this spin mismatch, enabling pressure-enhanced hybridization to drive a band inversion. The magnetization direction then controls the symmetries of the inverted bands and whether spin--orbit coupling produces a Chern-insulating gap or symmetry-protected nodal crossings. First-principles calculations for bilayer CrSBr illustrate this mechanism within a compressed orthorhombic structural model. Out-of-plane magnetization yields a Chern insulator with a chiral edge state, whereas in-plane magnetization supports a two-dimensional Weyl semimetal with node-connecting edge states. Continuous spin canting further demonstrates how magnetic reorientation can drive the transition and stabilize the Chern phase before full magnetic saturation. Although material-specific transition conditions depend on electronic correlations and structural stability under compression, the underlying strategy identifies interlayer hybridization as a link between magnetic order and band topology. These results provide a design principle for externally tunable topological phases in layered antiferromagnetic semiconductors.

title: Patient-specific Modeling of the Tricuspid Valve from 3D Transesophageal Echocardiography
abstract: Purpose: Image-based patient-specific simulations of the tricuspid valve (TV) could support repair planning. However, clinical images incompletely resolve the chordal anatomy and cannot directly determine tissue properties, which hinders the development of such models. We developed and evaluated a framework that simulates the TV from clinical images and addresses these limitations using measurements on explanted human valves. Methods: We reconstructed ten functionally competent human TVs from 3D transesophageal echocardiography. Following manual segmentation, we automatically built finite element models with synthetic chordae and with leaflet thickness, chordal insertion density, and tissue properties informed by ex vivo human measurements. Next, we used shape matching and force-based chordal-length adjustment to simulate valve closure. We also assessed inter-observer segmentation variability and sensitivity to chordal insertion density, leaflet stiffness, leaflet thickness, and chordal size and material properties. Results: Per-valve median geometric errors were 0.61-1.13 mm relative to the morphed references and 0.55-0.95 mm relative to the image-derived surfaces. Coaptation covered 20-42% of the leaflet area, and median leaflet stresses ranged from 7.6 to 16.9 kPa. Inter-observer variability in segmentation most strongly affected coaptation area. Of the population-based inputs, insertion density and leaflet stiffness most affected geometric error. Thickness primarily affected stress, whereas chordal size and material properties had limited effects. Conclusion: Clinical echocardiography, supplemented with ex vivo human tissue data, enabled patient-specific simulation of ten human TVs. This framework provides a foundation for investigating valve mechanics and developing repair-planning tools, while sensitivity analyses identify priorities for model refinement and uncertainty assessment.

title: Probing Non-Equilibrium Grain Boundary Dynamics with XPCS and Domain-Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: Grain-boundary (GB) dynamics control the stability, mechanical, and functional response of nanocrystalline materials, but direct experimental access to their slow non-equilibrium motion has been limited. Here we establish X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS), combined with domain-adaptive machine learning, as a quantitative probe of GB dynamics. Temperature- and grain-size-dependent two-time XPCS measurements in nanocrystalline silicon reveal pronounced departures from time-translation invariance, showing that GB relaxation can remain far from equilibrium over experimental timescales.

title: Combining five metals in one oxide improves ethanol gas sensing
abstract: A technology that significantly improves ethanol gas sensing performance by combining five different metal elements in a single oxide has been developed.

title: Water-activated polymer forms solid shapes underwater and bonds glass fragments
abstract: Cement hardens when mixed with water, allowing it to form solid structures even in wet environments. This property is known as hydraulicity. Reproducing this property in organic polymers has been challenging, as polymer materials that react with moisture often lack the combination of bulk curing and water resistance needed to harden reliably in wet conditions.

title: Interfacial Organization and Direction-Dependent Transport of Hydrocarbons in Graphene Slit Pores
abstract: Hydrocarbon transport in nanopores depends on the spatial organization of the confined fluid. We investigate this relationship through molecular dynamics simulations of methane, benzene, and n-octane between fixed graphene sheets, varying temperature and pore width. Density profiles and orientational distributions are combined with lateral mobility and wall-to-wall exchange to characterize structure and motion in interfacial and interior populations.

title: Understanding the Orchestrating Role of TLR2 in Differential Heterodimerization
EasyNMR: shareable flow-based workflows for reproducible analysis of NMR and other scientific data
abstract: Spectroscopic studies increasingly require analyses beyond what standard software offers, yet the programs that make them possible are often developed in single laboratories, are hard to maintain and are difficult to share. Here we present EasyNMR, a web-native platform that applies flow-based programming to the analysis of NMR spectra and other scientific data, turning each analysis into a shareable, executable workflow.

title: Comprehensive Two-dimensional liquid chromatography technology and its applications in the field of traditional Chinese medicine
abstract: Comprehensive two-dimensional liquid chromatography (LC×LC) represents a significant breakthrough in modern separation science.
